summary:
J.A.R.V.I.S. is an offline crew health monitor for long-duration missions, built as a wall display for a transit habitat. It replays open, real sensor recordings (MMASH, BIDMC and a wearable stress dataset) as the vitals of a fictional four-person crew, alongside simulated cabin CO2, and labels every value as real, derived or simulated.

Alarms come only from fixed, cited rules: NASA-STD-3001 CO2 limits, NEWS2 vital-sign bands, NASA sleep guidance and each astronaut's own baseline. When a rule fires, the screen moves to the affected person or module, a tone sounds and a voice reads the alarm. A local language model (Gemma via Ollama) then explains it in plain words and cites its evidence, but it never raises or clears an alarm. The crew can also ask JARVIS questions by voice or text.

Everything runs on board without internet, because a crew months from Earth cannot wait for ground support. JARVIS also catches patterns a single reading misses: when three crew in the same module report headaches as CO2 rises, it points to the air, not to three separate illnesses.
details:
What it does

J.A.R.V.I.S. is a crew health monitor that runs as a wall display inside a Mars transit habitat. At rest it shows an overview of the four crewmembers and the two habitat modules. When something goes wrong, the screen acts on its own:

  • A red alarm takes over the display immediately.
  • An amber alert waits until nobody is touching the screen.
  • A tone plays, and a voice reads the alarm aloud.
  • An acknowledgement on one screen counts for every screen.

Each crewmember has a profile with:

  • live vitals (heart rate, SpO2, breathing, skin temperature, HRV)
  • daily trends against their own personal baseline
  • a 3D body map showing where each sensor sits and which organ an alarm relates to

Crew can ask JARVIS questions by voice or text, for example "Who needs attention right now?"

How it works

JARVIS separates deciding from explaining:

  • Rules decide. Every alarm comes from a fixed, cited threshold:
    • NASA-STD-3001 limits for cabin CO2
    • NEWS2 bands for SpO2, breathing and heart rate
    • NASA OCHMO guidance for sleep
    • statistical drift from each person's own baseline
  • Alarm handling follows clinical patterns (IEC 60601-1-8, ISA-18.2): priorities, escalation, acknowledgement, and a hold time so alarms don't flicker at a threshold.
  • The AI only explains. A local language model writes a plain-language explanation that cites evidence cards (short findings from NASA standards and spaceflight studies). It never raises, grades or clears an alarm.

Real data drives the crew:

  • Open recordings are replayed as the crew's sensors: MMASH for heart rate, HRV, activity and sleep; BIDMC for SpO2 and breathing; a wearable stress and exercise dataset for skin temperature.
  • Values with no open source are simulated: cabin CO2, reaction time, blood pressure and mood.
  • Every value on screen is tagged REAL, DERIVED or SIMULATED.

Three scenarios show the system working:

  • CO2 slowly building up in the lab module
  • an oxygen saturation emergency
  • slow fatigue from poor sleep

A second console includes an investigation agent. It walks a crewmember through a symptom report, such as dizziness, with an emergency warning-sign check first.

Benefits

  • Works fully offline. A crew months from Earth, with up to 22 minutes of communication delay each way, cannot wait for ground support.
  • Trustworthy alarms. They come from published thresholds, not from a model's judgement, so they are predictable and auditable.
  • Catches what single readings miss. When three crew in the same module report headaches while CO2 rises, JARVIS points to the air, not to three separate illnesses. Each person is also compared with their own baseline, not with a population average.
  • Honest about its data. Nothing simulated is presented as real.

Intended impact

We want to show that onboard health monitoring can be autonomous without being a black box. Rules raise the alarm, and AI helps the crew understand it and decide what to check next. The approach also applies on Earth, wherever teams are far from a doctor: Antarctic stations, ships and remote clinics.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLite
  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Recharts, and three.js (React Three Fiber) for the 3D body map
  • Local AI: Ollama running Gemma (gemma4:e2b)
  • Offline voice: Faster Whisper for speech recognition, Piper for speech
  • Deployment: Docker Compose and Caddy on a Google Cloud VM, with a separate mission per visitor
    • PhysioNet: MMASH, BIDMC, Wearable Device Dataset
    • NASA OSDR: Inspiration4 studies OSD-569 and OSD-575
    • NASA-STD-3001 and NASA OCHMO technical briefs
    • Royal College of Physicians NEWS2
    • BodyParts3D for the anatomy model

How it is creative

  • It reasons about the environment, not only the patient: symptoms clustered in one module point to the air in that module.
  • It is a proactive wall display that moves to the problem by itself, instead of waiting for someone to open a dashboard.
  • The 3D body map connects each reading to where the sensor sits and which organ it concerns.
  • Real recordings from Earth are replayed as the crew's own sensors, with every value tagged by origin.

What our team considered

  • Safety: the language model never decides an alarm. If the model is unavailable, the rule-based explanation is shown instead.
  • Alarm fatigue: alarms are not repeated while a condition persists, heart-rate alarms are muted during exercise, and the screen returns home after a minute idle.
  • Privacy: all processing stays on board, and nothing leaves the habitat.
  • Usability: readable from two metres, operable by touch, with a voice that reads alarms aloud.
  • Honesty: every value is tagged by origin. The thresholds are demonstration settings and are not clinically validated, which we state on screen.

Trying the live demo

Open the link on a laptop or desktop with sound on and press Start mission. Each visitor gets their own mission, which plays the CO2 scenario in four chapters, from first symptoms to a red alarm. Press Continue to move to the next chapter.

JARVIS runs a local language model (Gemma via Ollama) on a single cloud VM, with no external AI service, the same way it would run on board. Answers can therefore take some time. The suggested questions are answered ahead of time and respond instantly. Any other question goes to the live model and can take up to 60 seconds. Alarms never wait for the model: they come from the rules and show at once.

The oxygen saturation and fatigue scenarios can be played after the CO2 scenario ends.
